summary: Extends Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) to TRILL switches, including integration with IP ECN, and provides ECN marking in the TRILL header. ECN lets forwarding elements signal congestion without dropping packets.

eli5.summary: Instead of throwing away mail when the post office is overloaded, workers mark it with a warning. This lets TRILL switches do that.

questions: what is the cce flag in trill
subtitle: How TRILL switches carry congestion warnings across a campus without dropping packets, and stay safe when some switches do not understand them.

tldr.problem: ECN lets a forwarding element signal the onset of congestion instead of dropping packets, but TRILL wraps frames in its own header, so IP ECN markings had no place to travel and TRILL switches had no way to mark congestion.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9600 defines a 2-bit TRILL-ECN field and a 1-bit CCE flag in the TRILL header extension flags word. The ingress copies IP ECN bits in, transit RBridges set CCE when congested, and the egress combines the markings with the inner header using a fixed table.
tldr.outcome: Congestion signals survive the trip across a TRILL campus, and if the egress does not understand ECN or the transport is not ECN-capable, the packet is dropped so congestion is still signalled.

today: RFC 9600 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2024, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the metadata. It builds on the guidelines in RFC 9599.

sections.title: Why TRILL Needs ECN
sections.content:
Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) lets a forwarding element tell downstream devices, including the destination, that congestion is starting, without dropping packets. The element marks a proportion of packets in an ECN field instead. IP headers have a 2-bit field for this.

TRILL encapsulates frames, often carrying IP, in a TRILL header. In the RFC's example, the ingress RBridge RB1 encapsulates and the egress RBridge RB9 decapsulates. A packet may already be marked by a forwarding element before RB1, and that marking is carried inside the encapsulation.

RFC 9600 specifies how the ingress copies ECN markings into the TRILL header extension flags word, how congested RBridges mark packets there, and how the egress merges everything so later hops can see congestion from anywhere on the path. It follows the guidelines for encapsulating protocols in RFC 9599.
sections.eli5: Imagine a package carried inside a bigger box. If a warning sticker is on the package, it must be copied onto the box, and put back on the package when the box is opened.

sections.title: The ECN Flags in the TRILL Header
sections.content:
The RFC defines two things inside the 32-bit TRILL header extension flags word: a 2-bit TRILL-ECN field and a 1-bit CCE (Critical Congestion Experienced) flag. TRILL-ECN uses bits 12 and 13, in the range reserved for non-critical hop-by-hop bits. CCE uses bit 26, in the range reserved for critical ingress-to-egress bits.

The first three TRILL-ECN codepoints mean the same as in the IP header: 00 Not-ECT, 01 ECT(1) and 10 ECT(0). The fourth, 11, is called NCCE (Non-Critical Congestion Experienced) so it is not confused with IP's CE.
sections.eli5: There are two little boxes on the shipping label: one says whether the sender can understand warnings, and one lights up when the package met a traffic jam.

sections.title: Ingress and Transit Behavior
sections.content:
An RBridge that supports ECN MUST follow the rules in Section 3 of the RFC. When encapsulating an IP frame, the ingress MUST set the F flag in the main TRILL header, create a flags word, copy the two ECN bits from the IP header into the TRILL-ECN field, and make sure CCE is zero. For a non-IP protocol with a way to indicate ECN, it follows Section 4.3 of RFC 9599.

Transit behavior is required at all RBridges where TRILL Data packets are queued. An RBridge that supports ECN MUST implement some form of active queue management (AQM) following RFC 7567. When the AQM decides to indicate critical congestion on a packet that has a flags word, it MUST set CCE. It does this without looking at the TRILL-ECN field.

If the packet has no flags word, the RBridge either drops it or MAY add one: set the F flag, add a flags word, set TRILL-ECN to Not-ECT (00), and set CCE and the CRItE summary bit.
sections.eli5: The first switch copies the warning sticker onto the outer box. Any busy switch on the way can light up the traffic-jam light, no matter what the sticker says.

sections.title: Egress Behavior and Dropping
sections.content:
If the egress does not support ECN, it ignores bits 12 and 13. If a transit RBridge set CCE, the egress still drops the packet, because dropping is the default for an RBridge that meets a CItE flag it does not understand. This is the behavior required by Section 4.4 of RFC 9599, and it means congestion is still signalled.

An ECN-capable egress decapsulating an IP packet MUST set the outgoing IP ECN field from Table 3. First it forms a 3-bit TRILL codepoint from TRILL-ECN and CCE: the result is CE if either NCCE or CCE is set, otherwise it keeps the TRILL-ECN name. With no flags word, the codepoint is taken as all zero bits.

If the TRILL codepoint indicates CE but the inner IP packet is Not-ECT, the egress MUST drop the packet, because a transport that is not ECN-capable only understands drops as congestion. Combinations marked with an asterisk are currently unused and SHOULD be logged. With one exception, Table 3 is consistent with IP-in-IP tunnels in RFC 6040; the exception is that the drop need not be logged.
sections.eli5: When the box is opened, the switch looks at both the box and the package. If there was a jam but the receiver cannot read warnings, the package is thrown away instead, which is its own way of saying slow down.

sections.title: Support for ECN Variants
sections.content:
Section 4 is informative. The wire protocol and the ingress and egress rules were designed to support other known ECN variants, and new variants have to follow the guidelines in RFC 4774.

PCN (Pre-Congestion Notification, RFC 6660) signals two levels of severity: CE as Excess-Traffic-Marked and ECT(1) as Threshold-Marked. On a transit RBridge, CCE would stand for Excess-Traffic-Marked and ECT(1) in TRILL-ECN for Threshold-Marked, with no change to ingress and egress rules.

For L4S (RFC 9331), the RFC says L4S is on the IETF's experimental track and gives pseudocode in Appendix A. In it a transit RBridge marks CCE with likelihood p squared and NCCE with likelihood p minus p squared in the L4S queue, so an ECN-capable egress propagates a CE mark with likelihood p, while an egress without ECN support drops CCE-marked packets with likelihood p squared.
sections.eli5: The warning-sticker system has room for fancier versions, like two kinds of warnings, without changing how the first and last switch work.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA updated the "TRILL Extended Header Flags" registry: bits 12-13 are now TRILL-ECN and bit 26 is Critical Congestion Experienced (CCE), both referencing RFC 9600.

The RFC says TRILL support of ECN is a straightforward combination of previously specified ECN and TRILL with no significant new security considerations. It points to RFC 9599 and RFC 6040 for general security considerations of adding ECN to lower-layer protocols, and to RFC 6325 for TRILL itself.
sections.eli5: The new stickers were added to the official list of label boxes. Since it only combines two systems that already existed, nothing new needs guarding.
